name: TPS54260DGQR
title: TPS54260: 2.5-A step-down converter for 3.5-V to 60-V inputs, with Eco-mode light-load pulse skipping
summary: A non-synchronous buck regulator for inputs from 3.5 V to 60 V with a built-in 200-mΩ high-side MOSFET switch and boot regulator; the catch diode is outside. It supplies up to 2.5 A. Peak current-mode control runs at a fixed frequency that one resistor sets anywhere from 100 kHz to 2.5 MHz, or locks to an outside clock between 300 kHz and 2.2 MHz; at light load it skips pulses (Eco-mode), drawing 138 µA regulated with no load and 1.3 µA with EN low. EN gives an adjustable UVLO with hysteresis, SS/TR sets slow start and allows tracking and sequencing, an open-drain PWRGD flags undervoltage and overvoltage, and frequency foldback and thermal shutdown protect it in overload. Packages: 10-pin HVSSOP (DGQ) and 10-pin 3 mm × 3 mm VSON (DRC), each with an exposed pad.
key_figures: 0.8 V; 0.784 V to 0.816 V over temperature

pins.name: BOOT
pins.function: Supply for the high-side gate drive; a capacitor goes from BOOT to PH. If that capacitor's voltage drops below what the switch needs, the switch is held off until it is recharged.

pins.name: EN
pins.function: Enable, pulled up by an internal current source. Open, the part runs; below 1.2 V it is off. Two resistors on EN set the input UVLO levels.

pins.name: SS/TR
pins.function: Slow start and tracking. A capacitor to ground sets the output rise time. The pin's voltage takes the place of the internal reference, so it also serves for tracking and sequencing.

pins.name: RT/CLK
pins.function: Timing resistor or clock input. With a resistor to ground, an internal amplifier holds the pin at a fixed voltage and the resistor sets the frequency. Pulled above the PLL upper threshold, the amplifier switches off and the pin becomes a high-impedance clock input to the PLL; when clock edges stop, resistor mode comes back.

pins.name: PWRGD
pins.function: Power-good output, open drain. Pulled low when the output is low through thermal shutdown, dropout, overvoltage, or EN shutdown.

pins.name: VSENSE
pins.function: Feedback input: the inverting node of the gm error amplifier.

pins.name: COMP
pins.function: Error-amplifier output and input to the switch-current comparator; the compensation network connects to COMP.

pins.name: PH
pins.function: Switch node: the source of the built-in high-side power MOSFET.

pins.name: POWERPAD
pins.function: Exposed thermal pad. The GND pin has to be connected to it on the board for the part to work properly.

circuits.title: 3.3-V output design example
circuits.description: A buck from 12 V nominal (10.8 V to 13.2 V) down to 3.3 V at up to 2.5 A, switching at 300 kHz set by R3 (412 kΩ). R1 and R2 on EN give a 6.0-V rising start and a 5.5-V falling stop. C3 sets the slow start, R5 and R6 scale the output down to the 0.8-V reference, and R4 with C5 makes a type 2A compensation network, C8 being left out. C4 feeds the high-side gate; D1 is the catch diode.
notes: The parts take about 0.55 in² of board, not counting test points or connectors.
D1 is a B360B-13-F (60 V); the input capacitors are 100-V parts.

circuits.title: Inverting power supply
circuits.description: A positive input made into a negative output by running the regulator with its GND pin on the negative rail. Lo goes from PH to system ground; the catch diode anode, the lower divider resistor and the IC's slow-start, timing and compensation parts all return to VOUT. Cd bypasses VIN to the IC's ground and Cin bypasses VIN to system ground. No values are given.
notes: EN is open, so the part is enabled, and PWRGD is unused. The exposed pad goes with the IC's GND pin, which in this circuit is VOUT.
TI application report SLVA317 treats this design at length.

circuits.title: Split-rail power supply
circuits.description: A positive input made into a positive and a negative output with a coupled inductor. The IC's GND pin sits on the negative output VONEG; Lo's first winding runs from PH to system ground, and its second winding charges Copos through D2 to make VOPOS. R1 and R2 sense from VOPOS to VONEG. No values are given.

parts.note: coupled inductor: winding 1 is pins 1-2 (dot at 1), winding 2 is pins 3-4 (dot at 4)

notes: EN is open and PWRGD is unused. The exposed pad goes with the IC's GND pin, which in this circuit is VONEG.
TI application report SLVA369 treats this design at length.

circuits.title: 12-V to 3.8-V GSM power supply
circuits.description: A supply for GSM-GPRS modules, whose load current jumps in large steps: 12 V nominal (8 V to 40 V) in, 3.8 V at 2.0 A out. R5 (237 kΩ) sets the frequency, R1 and R4 the EN undervoltage levels and R2 with R6 the output; R3, C8 and C6 compensate the loop.
notes: PWRGD is not connected.
TI application report SLVA412 treats these GSM-GPRS supplies at length.

circuits.title: 24-V to 4.2-V GSM power supply
circuits.description: The GSM-GPRS supply set up for 24 V nominal (18 V to 40 V) in and 4.2 V at 2.0 A out: R4 is 23.2 kΩ, one 100-µF output capacitor replaces two, the upper feedback resistor is 42.2 kΩ and the compensation capacitor C8 4700 pF.
notes: PWRGD is not connected.
TI application report SLVA412 treats these GSM-GPRS supplies at length.

circuits.title: Adjustable undervoltage lockout (UVLO)
circuits.description: R1 from VIN to EN and R2 from EN to ground set the input voltages at which the part starts and stops. They work against the EN pull-up current I1 and the hysteresis current Ihys that is added once EN passes 1.25 V (equations 2 and 3).
notes: Only VIN and EN of the IC take part.
The currents shown with this circuit are I1 = 1.18 µA and Ihys = 3.35 µA; the EN electrical characteristics give –0.9 µA and –2.9 µA, and equations 2 and 3 use 0.9 µA and 2.9 µA.

circuits.title: Adding additional hysteresis
circuits.description: The R1–R2 UVLO divider with a third resistor, R3, from the regulator output into EN. R3 feeds extra hysteresis current, for a wider hysteresis or when the two-resistor values come out too large (equations 4 and 5).
notes: Only VIN and EN of the IC take part.
The currents shown with this circuit are I1 = 1.18 µA and Ihys = 3.35 µA; the EN electrical characteristics give –0.9 µA and –2.9 µA.

circuits.title: Sequential start-up sequence
circuits.description: Two regulators brought up in turn: the open-drain PWRGD of the first pulls EN of the second, so the second starts once the first is regulating. Each has its own slow-start capacitor. A 1-nF ceramic capacitor on the second EN gives a 1-ms start-up delay where one is wanted.
notes: Only EN, SS/TR and PWRGD of each IC take part.

circuits.title: Ratiometric start-up sequence
circuits.description: Two regulators with their EN pins joined and their SS/TR pins joined on one slow-start capacitor, so both outputs ramp together and arrive at regulation together. Both pull-up currents charge the shared capacitor, so equation 6 is worked with twice the charge current.
notes: Only EN, SS/TR and PWRGD of each IC take part.

circuits.title: Ratio-metric and simultaneous start-up sequence
circuits.description: Two buck regulators sharing one EN line. The first ramps on its own slow-start capacitor C1; R1 and R2 divide its output VOUT1 into SS/TR of the second, so VOUT2 follows VOUT1. R3 and R4 set VOUT2. R1 and R2 come from equations 7 to 10: deltaV of zero makes both arrive together, a positive deltaV leaves VOUT2 slightly below VOUT1 at regulation, a negative one slightly above.
notes: Of each IC only EN, SS/TR, BOOT, PH and PWRGD take part, and on U2 also VSENSE.

circuits.title: Synchronizing to a system clock
circuits.description: An outside clock reaches RT/CLK through a 10-pF capacitor and a 4-kΩ series resistor. The frequency-set resistor Rfset runs from RT/CLK to the clock node, which 50 Ω holds to ground, so Rfset still sets the frequency if the clock stops. Rfset is picked for a frequency close to the clock's.
notes: Only RT/CLK of the IC takes part.

operation.text: Fixed-frequency peak current-mode control. Each cycle the oscillator turns the high-side switch on, and it turns off when switch current climbs to the level that COMP calls for; COMP rises and falls with load current. A top clamp on COMP sets the current limit and a bottom clamp gives Eco-mode. A compensating ramp added to the sensed current prevents subharmonic oscillation, and the peak current available is the same over the whole duty-cycle range.

Once the output is regulated, a cycle whose peak switch current falls below the skip threshold (the current that matches about 500 mV on COMP) stops switching, and COMP is held at 500 mV. The output droops, COMP climbs, and switching resumes on the next cycle until the peak current drops below the threshold again. Because peak current is what is sensed, the load at which skipping starts depends on the inductor; the 3.3-V example starts skipping near 5 mA. While idle it draws 138 µA; the PLL keeps running, so with an outside clock the skip pulses stay locked to it.

The boot regulator is inside; a 0.1-µF ceramic capacitor (X5R or X7R, 10 V or more) from BOOT to PH supplies the high-side gate and is recharged while the catch diode conducts. The switch may stay on at 100% duty for as long as BOOT-PH stays above 2.1 V; below that a UVLO turns it off so the capacitor can recharge. Little current is taken from the boot capacitor, so the switch can stay on for many cycles. At light or no load near dropout the inductor current can be too small to pull PH down and recharge the capacitor, and switching stops until VIN − VOUT is more than about 2.1 V; setting the VIN stop voltage with the EN divider above this point avoids it. At very high duty the output ripple grows, because the boot recharge time is longer than the normal off-time.

operation.topic: Start and stop voltages near dropout
operation.text: The start voltage is the input needed for the output to come within 1% of its setting; the stop voltage is the input at which the output drops 5% or switching stops.

A transconductance amplifier compares VSENSE with the lower of SS/TR and the 0.8-V reference. Its gm is 310 µS normally and 70 µS while VSENSE is below 0.8 V and the part regulates to SS/TR. The compensation network goes from COMP to ground.
The 0.8-V reference is a scaled temperature-stable bandgap, within ±2% over temperature.

A divider from the output to VSENSE sets the output (equation 1). Larger resistors raise light-load efficiency, but too large makes the loop prone to noise and lets the VSENSE input current cause visible error; at least 1 µA in the divider holds accuracy, which caps the lower resistor at 800 kΩ.

The part stops when VIN falls below 2.5 V. EN carries a 0.9-µA pull-up, so the part runs with EN open; once EN passes 1.25 V another 2.9 µA is added, giving hysteresis. Two resistors set the start and stop input voltages (equations 2 and 3); not required, but strongly advised for consistent power-up. A third resistor from the output into EN widens the hysteresis (equations 4 and 5).

Inside, EN has a 5.8-V zener behind 10 kΩ that can sink up to 100 µA, and that node must stay at or below 5.8 V. A low-impedance source above 5 V must not drive EN directly, and with a divider and VEN above 5 V there must be no capacitor straight on EN. EN may go above 5 V when the VIN source is high impedance and puts no more than 100 µA into EN.

Operation is recommended above 3.5 V. The typical VIN UVLO is 2.5 V and the part can run down to that level; below the actual UVLO it does not switch. With EN open or pulled above the 1.25-V typical threshold, it becomes active once VIN passes UVLO and starts with the slow-start ramp set by the SS/TR capacitor.

The enable start threshold is 1.25 V typical. With EN below it the part is off and does not switch even with VIN above UVLO, and its input current is reduced. Raising EN above the rising threshold with VIN above UVLO makes it active, and it starts with the slow-start ramp; pulling EN below 1.25 V again returns it to the low-current state.

The error amplifier uses the lower of SS/TR and the internal reference. A 2-µA source charges the SS/TR capacitor, so the capacitor sets the start time (equation 6). At power-up switching does not begin until SS/TR is below 40 mV; SS/TR is discharged to 40 mV the same way after a UVLO trip, EN pulled below 1.25 V, or thermal shutdown. Up to 85% of the reference VSENSE follows SS/TR with a 45-mV offset; beyond that the offset grows as control passes to the internal reference, a handover that is complete once SS/TR is above 1.3 V. SS/TR ramps linearly until clamped at 1.7 V.

When a fault drives the error amplifier high, a 382-µA pull-down brings SS/TR down to just above VSENSE. Once the fault clears, the output ramps back up from wherever it had fallen, as in a slow start.

Sequential start: PWRGD of one regulator, or any open-drain power-on reset output, drives EN of the next, so the second starts once the first is regulating; 1 nF on the second EN gives a 1-ms start-up delay. Ratiometric start: SS/TR pins joined make both outputs rise and arrive together, with the charge current doubled in equation 6. Ratio-metric or simultaneous tracking: a divider R1–R2 from the leading output into SS/TR of the following regulator, sized with equations 7 to 9; deltaV is zero for a simultaneous start and negative to have the second output end slightly above the first. R1 must be larger than equation 10 gives so the part can restart after a fault.

A resistor from RT/CLK to ground, where the pin sits near 0.5 V, sets the frequency from about 100 kHz to 2500 kHz (equation 11 or the RT curves). A higher frequency allows smaller parts, but efficiency, the highest input voltage and the 135-ns typical minimum on-time limit it, and frequency-shift protection limits it further.

The switch turns off each cycle when its current reaches the COMP level. In overload the output falls, COMP climbs to its internal clamp, and that clamp is the switch current limit. To hold inductor current in a short at high input, the frequency is divided by 8, 4, 2 and 1 as VSENSE rises from 0 V to 0.8 V, which lengthens the off-time so the current can ramp down. The division is digital, so it also works while synchronized to a clock. Since 8 is the largest divider, there is a highest input voltage up to which this protection holds.

Take the lower of equation 12 (the minimum on-time limit, above which pulses are skipped) and equation 13 (the limit for short-circuit protection with frequency shift, where fdiv goes from 1 to 8 as the output falls to 0 V). In the maximum-frequency curve the solid line is the frequency-shift limit, taken at 0 V output, 0.130 Ω inductor resistance, 0.2 Ω FET on-resistance and a 0.5-V diode drop; the dashed line is the pulse-skip limit.

A square wave on RT/CLK going below 0.5 V and above 2.2 V, high and low for more than 40 ns each, between 300 kHz and 2200 kHz, synchronizes the part; the PH rising edge follows the clock's falling edge. The clock is ac coupled through 10 pF and a 4-kΩ series resistor, and the frequency-set resistor, returned to ground through 50 Ω, is set near the clock frequency so the part keeps running if the clock stops. The series resistor reduces PH jitter at heavy load and on the change back to resistor mode. On the first clock edge above threshold the internal 0.5-V source is removed, the pin goes high impedance, and the PLL locks within 100 µs, moving up or down from the resistor frequency. When the clock stops, the frequency drops to 150 kHz, the 0.5 V returns and the resistor sets the frequency again. Synchronization holds in continuous, discontinuous and pulse-skip operation.

PWRGD is open drain. It is released when VSENSE is between 94% and 107% of the reference, and pulled low below 92% or above 109%, during UVLO or thermal shutdown, or with EN low. A pull-up of 10 kΩ to 100 kΩ to 5.5 V or less is advised. Its state is defined once VIN is above 1.5 V, with reduced sinking ability, reaching full sinking ability as VIN nears 3 V.

After an overload or a sudden load drop, the output can rise faster than the error amplifier can respond, most of all with small output capacitance. When VSENSE goes above 109% of the reference the high-side switch is held off; it can turn on again in the next clock cycle after VSENSE falls back below that level.
Above 182 °C junction the part stops switching. Once it cools below 182 °C it goes through a full power-up again, discharging SS/TR first.

For simulation the error amplifier is a voltage-controlled current source of 310 µS whose Ro and Co set its open-loop gain and bandwidth, and the power stage is a 10.5-S transconductance from COMP to switch current. The model holds in continuous conduction only. The control-to-output response has a dc gain, one pole that moves with load, and the ESR zero (equations 14 to 17); as load falls the gain rises and the pole moves lower, so the crossover stays about the same. High-ESR electrolytic output capacitors can reduce the compensation parts needed.

Three networks from COMP to ground suit the gm amplifier: type 2A (R3 in series with C1, plus C2 across them), type 2B (R3 and C1 only) and type 1 (C2 only). Type 2 suits wide-bandwidth designs with low-ESR output capacitors; type 1 suits high-ESR aluminium electrolytic or tantalum output capacitors (equations 18 to 27).

Equation 28 gives the least inductance. The ripple current is filtered by the output capacitor and has to be within its ripple rating. Keep the ripple above 150 mA; with a wide input range, lean toward more ripple so it remains measurable at low input. The inductor current can reach the switch current limit during start-up, faults or transients, so the most cautious choice is a saturation rating at or above the current limit. In the 3.3-V example KIND = 0.3 gives 11 µH, 10 µH is used, the RMS current is 2.51 A and the peak 2.913 A.

Three limits apply and the strictest sets the value: carrying a load step for about two cycles until the loop responds (equation 32), soaking up inductor energy on load release since the catch diode cannot sink current (equation 33), and ripple (equations 34 and 35). Ageing, temperature and dc-bias derating come on top. In the 3.3-V example these give 67 µF, 60 µF and 12 µF, with ESR below 36 mΩ; two 47-µF 10-V ceramics (3 mΩ each, 72.4 µF after derating) are used, with 238 mA of ripple current (equation 36).

A diode from PH to GND rated for at least the highest input voltage in reverse and for more than the peak inductor current, with a low forward voltage; Schottky types fit. At higher frequencies its junction-capacitance and recovery losses add to conduction loss (equation 37). The example uses a B360B-13-F, rated 60 V so input transients up to the TPS54260's rating are covered although the input only reaches 13.2 V; it has 0.70 V typical forward drop and 200 pF, and dissipates 1.32 W. Where the supply spends long stretches at light load or asleep, a diode with lower leakage and a slightly higher forward drop may suit better.

At least 3 µF of effective X5R or X7R ceramic capacitance, dc-bias loss included, rated above the highest input voltage and for the input ripple current (equation 38); bulk capacitance may be added. Input ripple follows equation 39. The example uses two 2.2-µF 100-V capacitors (4.4 µF), giving 473 mV of input ripple and 1.15 A RMS ripple current.

Slow start has to be long enough that charging the output capacitance needs no excessive current (equation 40), so the part does not hit current limit and the input does not sag. The example needs 0.19 ms to charge 72.4 µF to 3.3 V at 1 A average; it uses 3.5 ms, which needs 8.75 nF, rounded up to 10 nF.

With 13.2 V maximum input the skip limit is 2247 kHz; with a 0.7-V diode, 26-mΩ inductor, 200-mΩ switch, 3.5-A current limit and 0.2 V output in a short, the shift limit is about 4449 kHz. 300 kHz is used, set by 412 kΩ. The EN divider is 124 kΩ (VIN to EN) and 30.1 kΩ (EN to ground) for a 6.0-V start and 5.5-V stop. The lower feedback resistor is 10.0 kΩ; equation 1 gives 31.25 kΩ for the upper, rounded to 31.6 kΩ.

The method leaves out the internal slope compensation, so the real crossover usually comes out lower than calculated, and it assumes the crossover lies between the modulator pole and an ESR zero at least ten times higher. With a derated 40 µF the modulator pole is 1206 Hz and the ESR zero 530.5 kHz; equations 43 and 44 give 25.3 kHz and 13.4 kHz, and 35.0 kHz is chosen for a faster transient response. R4 comes to 20.2 kΩ (20.0 kΩ used) and C5 to 4740 pF (4700 pF used); the optional pole capacitor C8 is not fitted.
At 12 V in, the supply goes discontinuous below 337 mA of load and into Eco-mode below 5 mA; with no load it draws 392 µA from the input.

IC loss is conduction plus switching plus gate drive plus supply current (equations 49 to 53), in continuous conduction only; junction temperature and highest ambient follow from the package thermal resistance (equations 54 and 55). Losses in the inductor (ac and dc), the diode and the copper traces come on top.
The input supply should stay between 3.5 V and 60 V. If it is more than a few inches away, bulk capacitance besides the ceramics may be needed; 100 µF electrolytic is a typical choice.

Bypass VIN to ground with a low-ESR X5R or X7R ceramic and keep the loop of the bypass capacitor, VIN and the catch-diode anode small. Tie GND directly to the exposed pad, and the pad to inner ground planes with several vias right under the IC. PH is the switching node: route it to the diode cathode and the inductor, place both close, and keep its copper small to limit capacitive coupling. At full load the top-side ground has to give enough area to spread heat. RT/CLK picks up noise easily; its timing resistor sits as close to the IC as possible with short traces. The boot capacitor trace can run on another layer to leave a wide top-side ground path.
